lesson:
# Abstract syntax trees for HDLs

An abstract syntax tree (AST) keeps the structure of a program and drops the punctuation that only served to fix that structure. It is the first real data structure of a hardware compiler: Yosys's Verilog front end builds one, slang builds a richer one, and elaboration, type checking and lowering to netlist IRs all walk it. Counting its nodes, its height and its shared subtrees exercises what a compiler stores.

## Nodes of an expression tree

In an expression AST every operator is an internal node whose children are its operands, and every operand occurrence is a leaf. Parentheses produce no node: their only job was to choose the shape, which the tree records directly. A unary operator has one child, a binary operator two, and the conditional ?: is one node with three children.

So (t ? (2 & c) : a) ^ ~(a - d) has the operators ^, ?:, &, ~ and -, five internal nodes, and the leaf occurrences t, 2, c, a, a and d, six leaves, for 11 nodes in all. Note that a appears twice as a leaf: an AST is a tree, so a repeated operand is a repeated node. A concrete syntax tree, by contrast, would keep every token, parentheses included.

## Height and traversal

The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. The root is the operator applied last, the loosest-binding one at the top level. For (1 ^ b) ^ (1 - c), the root ^ has two children of height 1, so the tree has height 2. For an expression tree the height is the depth of nesting, which for a combinational circuit built directly from it is the number of logic levels on the longest path.

Compilers walk ASTs in two orders. A post-order traversal visits children before their parent, which is how an evaluator or a code generator processes operands before the operator. A pre-order traversal visits the parent first, which is how attributes such as expected widths are pushed down, exactly the two passes Verilog's sizing rules require.

## Sharing subtrees in a DAG

Identical subtrees compute identical values, so a compiler can store each one once. Hash-consing does this: before creating a node, look up its operator and the identities of its children in a table, and reuse an existing node if one matches. The tree becomes a directed acyclic graph.

In ((2 - d) * (b ^ 1)) | (c + (2 - d)) the tree has 13 nodes. The subtree 2 - d appears twice and becomes one node, and the leaves 2 and d are shared with it, as is every repeated operand. The DAG has 10 nodes. This is common subexpression elimination performed at construction time, and it is the representation behind and-inverter graphs in ABC and the structural hashing done by every logic synthesizer. Two subtrees match only if they are written identically, operand order included, unless the compiler first puts commutative operators into a canonical order.

## Going deeper

Appel, "Modern Compiler Implementation in ML", chapter 4; Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-Aware AIG Rewriting" (DAC 2006).

label: Elaboration
lesson:
# Elaboration

Elaboration turns a set of parsed modules into one concrete design. It picks the top, links every instance to its module, evaluates parameters and widths per instance, unrolls generate constructs and builds the instance tree. It is the phase where HDL compilers differ most and where SystemVerilog is hardest to implement, which is why shared elaborators such as slang and Surelog exist.

## What elaboration builds

Parsing checks each file against the grammar on its own. Elaboration starts from the top module and builds the design: it resolves each instance to its module definition, binds parameter values, evaluates every constant expression in declarations (so a port declared [W-1:0] gets a number), unrolls generate loops and selects generate-if branches. The result is a tree of instances in which nothing is symbolic any more.

Only what is reachable from the top is elaborated. A module that is parsed but never instantiated under the chosen top is not part of the design, although some tools treat every uninstantiated module as an extra top, which is why flows name the top explicitly. The elaborated design is what simulation and synthesis consume.

## Parameters resolve top down

A child's parameters can depend on values its parent passes in, so elaboration resolves the hierarchy top down: the parent's values are known before the child is specialized. Two instances of fifo with W = 8 and W = 16 become two specializations of fifo, one per distinct parameter set; tools name them separately (Yosys uses a paramod prefix). A generate-if on a parameter is decided per instance, so only one implementation exists for each.

defparam complicates this, because it can override a parameter from anywhere in the hierarchy, making the result depend on resolution order. Modern guidelines and tools discourage it in favor of inline #() overrides, which keep every override local to the instance it affects.

## Errors that only elaboration can see

Some errors are invisible until the design is assembled. Every file can parse cleanly while an instance names a module that no file defines. A port connection's width mismatch is only detectable once a parameter fixes the port width. Recursive instantiation terminates only if a parameter-dependent generate condition eventually fails, as when N is halved down to 1.

Because elaboration is where SystemVerilog's semantics live, building a complete elaborator is a large project. Surelog and slang each build a full elaborated model, and Surelog writes it out as UHDM so that other tools (a Yosys plug-in, Verilator, CIRCT) can consume one shared interpretation instead of implementing their own. That sharing matters because two elaborators that disagree produce two different designs from the same source.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 23.10 (elaboration) and clause 27 (generate constructs); the slang and Surelog documentation.

lesson:
# Parameters and parameter overrides

Parameters make one module definition describe a family of hardware: a FIFO of any depth, a bus of any width. Elaboration binds a value to every parameter of every instance and evaluates every expression that depends on them, including port widths. Front ends must get the override rules exactly right, because a wrong width propagates silently into synthesis and simulation.

## Defaults and named overrides

A module declares parameters with defaults: module buffer #(parameter DEPTH = 16, parameter W = 8). A localparam such as localparam PW = W + 2*DEPTH; is derived and cannot be overridden from outside, which makes it the right place for values that must stay consistent with the others. Port widths can use both, as in output [PW-1:0] bus.

An instance overrides parameters by name: buffer #(.W(12)) u0 (...); sets W to 12 and leaves DEPTH at its default. Elaboration then evaluates the localparam for this instance, $PW = 12 + 2 \times 16 = 44$, and the bus port of u0 is 44 bits wide. Every instance is evaluated separately, so two instances with different overrides have different port widths.

## Values passed down the hierarchy

Overrides can be expressions over the parent's own parameters. If core #(parameter N = 2) instantiates buffer #(.DEPTH(N*2), .W(N+3)), and top instantiates core #(.N(6)), elaboration resolves top down: u_core gets N = 6, then u_buf gets DEPTH = 12 and W = 9, so PW = $9 + 2 \times 12 = 33$.

The order is forced: a child cannot be specialized until its parent's values are known. This is why elaboration is a top-down tree walk, and why the older defparam statement, which can override a parameter from anywhere in the hierarchy, makes the result depend on resolution order and is discouraged. Each distinct set of parameter values produces one specialized module, which later stages treat as a separate definition.

## Positional overrides

An instance can also override parameters by position: buffer #(6, 10) u0 (...); assigns the values in the order the parameters are declared in the module header. With the header #(parameter DEPTH = 4, parameter W = 8) this sets DEPTH = 6 and W = 10, giving $PW = 10 + 2 \times 6 = 22$; if the header declared W first, the same instance would set W = 6 and DEPTH = 10, giving $6 + 20 = 26$.

Positional binding therefore couples every instance to the declaration order of the module, and reordering parameters in a header silently changes every positional instance. Named overrides avoid this, which is why style guides and linters prefer them. A front end must also reject attempts to override a localparam and report overrides of parameters that do not exist, both common symptoms of a mismatch between an instance and its module.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Generate loops and conditional generate

Generate constructs build hardware structure at elaboration time: a loop that creates one instance per bit, a nested loop that builds a systolic array, a conditional that picks an implementation from a parameter. Elaboration evaluates them completely, so the elaborated design contains only the instances they produce. Counting those instances is the same computation the elaborator performs.

## Generate loops

A generate loop uses a genvar, a variable that exists only during elaboration. for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin : g ... end creates one copy of its body for each value of i, named g[0] to g[7], and inside each copy i is a constant. The loop never becomes hardware; only its copies do.

Counting copies is counting iterations. With start s, bound e and step k, the loop with i < e runs $\lceil (e - s) / k \rceil$ times when $e > s$, and the loop with i <= e runs $\lfloor (e - s) / k \rfloor + 1$ times. So for (i = 0; i <= 10; i = i + 1) creates 11 instances, and for (i = 2; i < 17; i = i + 3) creates 5, at i = 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14. Named blocks matter: the label g gives each copy a stable hierarchical name such as g[3].u.

## Nested loops with conditions

Generate loops nest, and a generate-if inside them keeps only the copies whose condition holds. A two-dimensional processing array with for i < 3 and for j < 4 and the condition (i + j) % 2 == 0 enumerates 12 (i, j) pairs and keeps 6. A triangular condition such as j <= i over $n \times n$ pairs keeps $n(n+1)/2$.

The condition is evaluated per copy during elaboration, so it may use genvars and parameters but nothing that changes at run time. This is how designers build structures such as the upper triangle of a matrix unit or the boundary cells of a mesh, and it is why elaborated designs can have very different instance counts from what the source text suggests.

## Parameter-dependent structures

Bounds can depend on parameters and on outer genvars. A reduction tree of two-input adders over N inputs, with level l creating N >> (l + 1) adders for $l = 0, 1, \dots, L - 1$, builds $N/2 + N/4 + \dots$ adders. With N = 24 and L = 2 the levels contribute 12 and 6, so 18 adders. For N a power of two and $L = \log_2 N$ the total is $N - 1$, the familiar count for a binary tree.

Because the structure depends on parameters, the same module elaborates to different hardware for each instance, and each distinct parameter set is a separate specialization. Recursion through generate-if, where a module instantiates smaller copies of itself until a base case, is the other common pattern, and it terminates only because elaboration evaluates the condition with constants.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Chisel and embedded hardware DSLs

Chisel is a hardware construction language embedded in Scala, and it stands for a broader idea: describing hardware with a program that generates it. Running the program elaborates the circuit, which is emitted as FIRRTL and compiled to Verilog. Embedded DSLs such as Chisel, Amaranth, SpinalHDL and Clash change where parameterization lives and what a hardware compiler receives as input.

## Generators embedded in a host language

A Chisel design is a Scala program. Executing it constructs a graph of hardware: modules, registers, wires and operators. Scala control flow runs at elaboration time, before any hardware exists, so a Scala for loop that creates eight adders is the analogue of a Verilog generate loop, and a Scala if decides which hardware to build at all. A Chisel when, by contrast, builds hardware (multiplexers) that chooses at run time. Confusing the two is the classic embedded-DSL bug.

Embedding gives generators the host language for free: types, functions, higher-order combinators, collections and libraries. A parameterized family of designs, such as a configurable cache or a systolic array, becomes an ordinary program, checked by the host compiler before any hardware is emitted.

## Connection semantics and widths

Chisel and FIRRTL use last-connect semantics: if a wire is connected unconditionally twice, x := a and later x := b, the second connection wins and x carries b. Inside a when block, a later connection overrides only under that condition, which is how conditional assignment becomes a multiplexer.

Reg creates a register on the module's implicit clock with no reset; RegInit adds a reset value. Widths may be left unspecified and are inferred. The plain + truncates to the larger operand width, while +& keeps the carry, so adding two 8-bit values with +& gives 9 bits. A wire that is never connected is reported as not fully initialized unless it is explicitly marked DontCare, which turns a forgotten connection into a compile error instead of a silent x.

## The landscape of hardware DSLs

Other embedded DSLs make similar trade-offs in different hosts. Amaranth (formerly nMigen) is embedded in Python; SpinalHDL in Scala; Clash takes another approach, compiling a subset of Haskell functions into circuits so that the functional program is the circuit itself. High-level synthesis tools sit further away, scheduling untimed C++ into RTL.

Every DSL ends in generated Verilog, because that is what simulators, synthesis and timing tools consume. Debugging therefore happens partly in the generated code: timing reports and waveforms name Verilog signals, so stable names and source locators in the emitted output are what connect a report back to the generator. A generator pays off when the design is a family of variants; for a single fixed block, the extra layer may cost more than it saves.

## Going deeper

Bachrach et al., "Chisel: Constructing Hardware in a Scala Embedded Language" (DAC 2012); the Chisel and Amaranth documentation.

label: Intermediate representations for hardware
lesson:
# Intermediate representations for hardware

An intermediate representation (IR) is the form a compiler transforms between parsing and output. Hardware compilers use several, from process-level IRs that still contain branches, through word-level netlists, to bit-level and-inverter graphs. Choosing what each level keeps (words, names, processes, registers) decides which optimizations are easy, which is the central design decision of any synthesis or simulation tool.

## Why compilers lower the AST

An AST mirrors source syntax: there are dozens of statement and expression forms, and many ways to write the same hardware. An IR gives a small, uniform vocabulary, such as cells connected by nets or SSA operations with explicit operands, that passes can analyze and rewrite without caring how the source was written. Most hardware IRs are graphs: operations or cells are nodes, and the values or nets connecting them are edges.

The level of the IR fits the optimization. Logic optimization by rewriting works best on an and-inverter graph, a bit-level graph of two-input AND nodes with inverted edges, which is what ABC rewrites. Datapath optimization needs word-level operators, such as a 32-bit add or a multiplexer, which a bit-level graph has already dissolved.

## Levels and progressive lowering

Real flows lower through several levels. Yosys keeps procedural code as processes in RTLIL until the proc passes convert them into multiplexers and flip-flops; then word-level cells are optimized; then techmap lowers them to single-bit gates; then ABC works on an AIG. MLIR-based compilers such as CIRCT make this explicit as progressive lowering through dialects. Each step is small, so it is easy to test and to reason about.

Two kinds of information must survive lowering. Registers must stay explicit, because they separate cycles: combinational optimization works within a cycle, and moving state (retiming) is a deliberate, separate transformation. Source names and locations must travel as attributes, so that a timing report or a lint warning on a netlist cell can be traced back to an RTL line.

## SSA, verifiers and text formats

Many modern IRs use static single assignment: every value has exactly one definition, so use-def chains are explicit and dataflow optimizations are simple. A combinational netlist is already close to SSA, since every net has exactly one driver; registers break cycles the way phi functions merge values at loop headers.

Two engineering properties make an IR practical. A textual, round-trippable format, such as RTLIL text or MLIR assembly, lets an engineer dump a pass's input and output, diff them and replay the pass alone, which is how regression tests for compiler passes are written. A verifier that checks well-formedness after every pass catches a malformed IR at the pass that created it rather than many passes later. Both matter even more when passes are written or modified automatically.

## Going deeper

Wolf, "Yosys Manual", chapters on RTLIL and the synthesis flow; Lattner et al., "MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure for Domain Specific Computation" (CGO 2021).

# Control-flow graphs and basic blocks

A control-flow graph (CFG) represents procedural code as basic blocks connected by possible transfers of control. It is the substrate of every compiler analysis that follows: dominators, SSA construction and data-flow analysis. Hardware compilers need it for the procedural parts of HDLs (always blocks, functions, tasks and testbench code) before those parts become multiplexers and registers.

## Basic blocks

A basic block is a maximal sequence of statements that execute together: control enters only at the first statement and leaves only after the last. A new block starts at the target of every branch and at every join point. A condition such as if (a > 2) is the last statement of the block that evaluates it, because control may go two ways after it.

Count blocks structurally. Straight-line code is one block. An if-then adds two: the then block and the join block that follows. An if-else adds three: two arms and the join. A while loop adds three: a header that evaluates the condition, the body and the exit block after the loop. For d = a + 1; a = a + 1; if (i < 6) begin s = c + 4; end c = d + 5;, there are three blocks: the entry block ending with the test, the then block, and the join block.

## Edges

An edge goes from block b to block c when control can pass directly from the end of b to the start of c. An if-then has three edges: test block to then block, test block to join (the false path) and then block to join. An if-else has four: two out of the test and one from each arm into the join. A while loop has four: into the header, header to body, the back edge from the end of the body to the header, and header to exit.

The back edge is what makes a loop: it points to a block that dominates its source. Nested constructs compose, because the inner construct's join or exit block becomes the current block of the outer one. In the CFG of an if-else whose then arm contains an if-then, there are six blocks and seven edges.

## Cyclomatic complexity

For a connected CFG with $N$ blocks and $E$ edges, the cyclomatic complexity is $M = E - N + 2$, the number of linearly independent paths through the code. For structured code with one entry and one exit, it equals the number of decisions plus one: every if and every while adds one. Six blocks and seven edges give $M = 3$, matching two decisions.

The number has practical uses: it bounds the number of test paths needed for branch coverage and flags overly complex procedures. In hardware, procedural complexity also predicts the size of the multiplexer trees that synthesis builds from a combinational block. Compilers build the CFG once and run every later analysis on it, so getting block boundaries right is the foundation of everything that follows.

## Going deeper

Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, "Compilers", section 8.4 (basic blocks and flow graphs); McCabe, "A Complexity Measure" (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 1976).

label: Static single assignment
lesson:
# Static single assignment

Static single assignment (SSA) is the form in which every variable is assigned exactly once. Renaming each assignment to a fresh version makes use-def chains explicit, and phi functions merge versions where control flow joins. Nearly every modern compiler IR, including LLVM and MLIR, is SSA, and hardware netlists are naturally close to it, so SSA is the bridge between procedural HDL code and circuits.

## Renaming straight-line code

In straight-line code, give each assignment to a variable the next version number and rewrite each read to name the most recent version above it. With x's incoming value as $x_0$, the code x = x + w; x = z + z; z = y + 4; becomes $x_1 = x_0 + w_0$, $x_2 = z_0 + z_0$, $z_1 = y_0 + 4$. A later read of z refers to $z_1$, and a read of x to $x_2$.

This is exactly what blocking assignments mean in a combinational always block: each write creates a new value, and later statements read it. Synthesis tools perform this renaming when they turn a process into logic: every version becomes a net, and the final versions drive the block's outputs. Nonblocking assignments, in contrast, read the pre-edge values, all version 0.

## Phi functions at joins

When control joins, a variable may arrive with different versions from different predecessors. After if (sel) z = y + y; else w = z + 9;, z arrives as $z_1$ from the then arm and $z_0$ from the else arm. SSA inserts $z_2 = \phi(z_1, z_0)$ at the join, which selects the version from whichever edge was taken. In hardware this phi is exactly a multiplexer controlled by sel.

Minimal SSA places a phi at the join for every variable assigned in at least one arm, because two different definitions meet there; a variable assigned in neither arm needs none. In an if/else where the arms assign {z, y} and {w}, minimal SSA places three phis: for w, y and z.

## Pruned SSA

Minimal SSA may place phis whose results are never used. Pruned SSA places a phi only for a variable that is live at the join, meaning some path from the join reads the variable before overwriting it. If the code after the join is x = y + z; z = z + x; and nothing later reads w, then w's phi is dead: pruned SSA omits it, while y and z, if assigned in an arm, keep theirs because they are read.

Computing pruned SSA requires liveness, a backward data-flow analysis, which costs compile time but saves IR size. Many compilers build minimal SSA and let dead-code elimination remove useless phis afterwards. In hardware terms, a dead phi is a multiplexer driving nothing, which opt_clean in Yosys would sweep.

## Going deeper

label: Dominators and dominance frontiers
lesson:
# Dominators and dominance frontiers

In a control-flow graph, block d dominates block v when every path from the entry to v passes through d. Dominance gives a tree over the CFG and a frontier where each block's influence ends. These are the inputs to SSA construction, loop detection and many optimizations, so every compiler, hardware compilers included, computes them early and reuses them.

## Dominator sets

Block d dominates v, written d dom v, when every path from the entry block to v includes d. Every block dominates itself, and the entry dominates every block. The sets satisfy a fixed-point equation: $\text{Dom}(\text{entry}) = \{\text{entry}\}$ and, for every other block, $\text{Dom}(v) = \{v\} \cup \bigcap_{p \in \text{pred}(v)} \text{Dom}(p)$.

Solve it by iteration: start with every non-entry set equal to all blocks, then repeatedly apply the equation until nothing changes. With edges 1→2, 1→3, 1→4, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5, 4→6, block 4 has predecessors 1 and 2, so $\text{Dom}(4) = \{4\} \cup (\{1\} \cap \{1, 2\}) = \{1, 4\}$, and block 6, whose only predecessor is 4, has $\text{Dom}(6) = \{1, 4, 6\}$.

## Immediate dominators and the tree

The strict dominators of v (its dominators other than itself) are totally ordered along every path from the entry. The closest one is the immediate dominator, idom(v): the strict dominator that every other strict dominator of v also dominates. In a set such as $\text{Dom}(3) = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the immediate dominator is 2, the strict dominator with the largest dominator set of its own.

Linking each block to its immediate dominator gives the dominator tree, rooted at the entry. Practical compilers compute it directly with the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm or with the simpler iterative algorithm of Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy, which runs over blocks in reverse postorder and is fast on real CFGs. A back edge is an edge whose target dominates its source, which is how natural loops are found.

## Dominance frontiers

The dominance frontier of v, DF(v), is the set of blocks w where v dominates a predecessor of w but does not strictly dominate w itself: the first places where v's dominance ends. With edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5, block 3 dominates the predecessor 3 of block 5 but not 5, so DF(3) = {5}; likewise DF(4) = {5}, and DF(2) is empty because 2 dominates 5.

A simple algorithm finds frontiers from joins: for every block b with two or more predecessors, walk up the dominator tree from each predecessor until reaching idom(b), adding b to the frontier of every block passed. A block on a loop can be in its own frontier, through the back edge. Frontiers are exactly where SSA construction must place phi functions, which is why they matter.

## Going deeper

Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy, "A Simple, Fast Dominance Algorithm" (2001); Lengauer and Tarjan, "A Fast Algorithm for Finding Dominators in a Flowgraph" (TOPLAS 1979).

label: Placing phi functions with dominance frontiers
lesson:
# Placing phi functions with dominance frontiers

Constructing SSA form requires knowing where to put phi functions. The classical answer, due to Cytron and colleagues, is the iterated dominance frontier of the blocks that assign each variable. It places the minimum number of phis that minimal SSA needs, and it is the algorithm behind SSA construction in many compilers; MLIR expresses the same merges as block arguments.

## One definition block: the dominance frontier

If variable v has a value on entry and is assigned again in block d, the new definition reaches every block that d dominates without competition. The first blocks where it competes with another definition are exactly the blocks of DF(d): there, some predecessors carry d's version and others carry an older one, so a phi is needed.

With edges 1→2, 1→4, 2→3, 3→4, 3→5 and assignments to v in blocks 3 and 5, DF(3) = {4} (block 4 also receives the entry version via 1→4) and DF(5) is empty, since block 5 has a single predecessor and no successors. Minimal SSA places one phi, in block 4. The entry block never contributes, because it dominates everything and its frontier is empty.

## Iterating the frontier

A phi is itself a new definition of the variable. Placing a phi in block w can therefore require more phis at DF(w), and so on. The set of phi blocks is the iterated dominance frontier $\text{DF}^+(S)$ of the definition set S: the limit of $\text{DF}_1 = \text{DF}(S)$, $\text{DF}_{i+1} = \text{DF}(S \cup \text{DF}_i)$. A worklist computes it: start with the definition blocks, and whenever a block gains a phi, add it to the worklist so that its frontier is processed too.

Loops are where iteration shows. With a back edge 3→2 and definitions in blocks 2 and 4, the back edge puts block 2 in DF(2) and DF(3), and the join at block 4 is in DF(2) as well, so phis go to blocks 2 and 4. The loop header needs a phi because it merges the entry version with the version coming around the loop.

## Several variables and pruning

Phi placement is done per variable, each with its own definition blocks, and the totals add. If u is assigned in blocks 3 and 7 and v in blocks 4 and 5 of the same CFG, their phi sets are computed independently, and the total count is the sum of the two set sizes. The dominance frontiers are computed once and shared, which is why the algorithm is efficient: roughly linear in the size of the program plus the number of phis placed.

Minimal SSA can place phis for variables that are dead at the join. Pruned SSA filters the iterated frontier by liveness, and semi-pruned SSA skips variables that are never live across a block boundary. MLIR represents the result differently but equivalently: instead of a phi at the top of block w, block w takes a block argument and each branch into w passes the value, which makes the edge-to-value pairing explicit.

## Going deeper

Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman and Zadeck, "Efficiently Computing Static Single Assignment Form and the Control Dependence Graph" (TOPLAS 1991); Appel, "Modern Compiler Implementation", chapter 19.

label: Data-flow analysis
lesson:
# Data-flow analysis

Data-flow analysis computes facts that hold at every point of a program, such as which definitions may reach a point or which variables may still be read later, by solving equations over the control-flow graph to a fixed point. It is the engine behind constant propagation, dead-code elimination, register inference and latch detection, and its theory (lattices and monotone transfer functions) explains why iteration terminates.

## Reaching definitions

A definition d reaches a point p if some path from d to p does not redefine d's variable. For each block, GEN is the last definition of each variable in the block, and KILL is every other definition of those variables. The equations are $\text{IN}[b] = \bigcup_{p \in \text{pred}(b)} \text{OUT}[p]$ and $\text{OUT}[b] = \text{GEN}[b] \cup (\text{IN}[b] - \text{KILL}[b])$, with IN of the entry empty. It is a forward may-analysis: facts flow along edges, and a union merges them.

Take blocks 1 (d1: b), 2 (d2: c, then d3: b), 3 (d4: b) and 4 (d5: b), with edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4, 4→2. Iterating gives OUT[1] = {d1}, OUT[2] = {d2, d3}, OUT[4] = {d2, d5}, so IN[2] = {d1, d2, d5}. This is the analysis that decides whether a variable in a process is assigned on every path, which is exactly latch detection.

## Liveness

A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it. Liveness runs backward: $\text{OUT}[b] = \bigcup_{s \in \text{succ}(b)} \text{IN}[s]$ and $\text{IN}[b] = \text{USE}[b] \cup (\text{OUT}[b] - \text{DEF}[b])$, where USE is the set of upward-exposed reads, read before any write in the block, and DEF the set of variables written. Nothing is live after the exit.

Liveness answers practical questions in hardware compilers. A blocking temporary in a clocked block that is live on entry to the block is read before it is written, so it needs a flip-flop. A phi whose variable is dead at a join can be pruned. And a register whose value is never live anywhere can be removed.

## Lattices and termination

Why does iteration stop? The facts at each point form a lattice, here the subsets of a finite set ordered by inclusion, and the transfer functions are monotone: a larger input never yields a smaller output. Starting from the empty set and applying monotone functions, each set can only grow, and it can grow only finitely often, so a fixed point is reached; it is the least solution of the equations.

The same framework covers many analyses by changing the lattice, the direction and the merge. Available expressions is a forward must-analysis with intersection; constant propagation uses a lattice of unknown, a constant value and not-a-constant. Visiting blocks in a good order (reverse postorder for forward problems) makes most real CFGs converge in a few passes, and loops are what require more than one. A worklist algorithm revisits only the blocks whose inputs changed.

## Going deeper

Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, "Compilers", chapter 9; Nielson, Nielson and Hankin, "Principles of Program Analysis", chapter 2; Kildall, "A Unified Approach to Global Program Optimization" (POPL 1973).

label: Hierarchy flattening and uniquification
lesson:
# Hierarchy flattening and uniquification

After elaboration a design is a tree of instances. Flattening replaces each instance with a copy of its module's contents, so the whole design becomes one module; uniquification gives each distinct specialization its own definition. Both change what later optimizations can see and how large the netlist becomes, so tool builders must be able to predict their effect exactly.

## Counting copies after flattening

Flattening copies a module once for every path from the top to an instance of it. If top contains 4 alu instances and 3 ctrl instances, each alu contains 2 regfile instances and each ctrl contains 3, the flat netlist contains $4 \times 2 + 3 \times 3 = 17$ copies of regfile's logic. The count is the number of root-to-leaf paths in the instance tree that end at regfile, found by multiplying instance counts along each path and summing over the paths.

Hierarchical names survive as part of the flattened names, typically joined with dots, such as alu_2.rf_1.mem, so reports can still be traced to the original hierarchy. Yosys's flatten pass performs this inlining, leaving black boxes and modules marked keep_hierarchy in place.

## Counting cells in the flat module

The size of the flat netlist follows from a bottom-up sum. Each module's total is its own primitive cells plus the totals of its children times their instance counts. With top 12 cells, alu 34 cells and 3 regfiles, ctrl 8 cells and 3 regfiles, regfile 18 cells, 2 alus and 1 ctrl: alu totals $34 + 3 \times 18 = 88$, ctrl totals $8 + 54 = 62$, and the flat module has $12 + 2 \times 88 + 62 = 250$ cells.

This is a post-order traversal of the module DAG, computed once per definition rather than once per instance, which matters for large designs: the flat netlist can be far larger than the source suggests. That growth is the cost of flattening; the benefit is that constants and duplicate logic across former boundaries become visible to optimization.

## Uniquification by parameter set

Before flattening, elaboration already creates one module definition per distinct parameter assignment. Instances that agree on every parameter value share one specialization: two fifo instances with default parameters share the original fifo, while fifo #(.W(32), .DEPTH(8)) and fifo #(.W(16)) each need their own. A design whose top contains ctrl twice, fifo twice with defaults and one fifo with W = 32 and DEPTH = 8 has four module definitions: top, ctrl, fifo and the specialized fifo.

Uniquification goes one step further when instances of the same specialization are later optimized differently, for example because their inputs are tied to different constants: each must become a separate definition first. Flattening makes the question moot by copying everything, which is one reason synthesis scripts flatten before the main optimization passes.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual entries for hierarchy, flatten and uniquify; IEEE Std 1800-2017, clause 23.

label: Constant propagation and folding
prereqs: Expression bit widths under Verilog sizing rules
lesson:
# Constant propagation and folding

Constant propagation replaces values known at compile time by their constants and folds the operations that use them. In hardware compilers it is the most productive single optimization: tied-off inputs, parameter-dependent logic and configuration bits all become constants, and folding them deletes logic. Yosys runs it as opt_expr; MLIR runs it as folding during canonicalization.

## Folding forward through SSA

In SSA form each value has one definition, so propagation is a single forward pass: if both operands of an operation are known constants, evaluate it at compile time and record the result as a constant for every later use. With x an unknown input, t1 = 1 + 2; t2 = t1 * 3; t3 = t2 + x; gives t1 = 3, then t2 = 9, while t3 stays an operation because x is unknown; it becomes t3 = 9 + x.

In hardware the effect is concrete. A constant operand turns an adder into a narrower or simpler circuit, a constant multiplexer select removes the multiplexer and one of its input cones, and a constant register input with a matching reset value removes the register. Synthesis flows run folding repeatedly, because each round can expose new constants.

## Algebraic identities

Plain folding needs every operand constant, but some identities produce constants from unknown values: $v \cdot 0 = 0$, $v \wedge 0 = 0$ (bitwise AND), $v \vee \bar{0} = $ all ones, $v \oplus v = 0$. Others simplify without producing constants: $v + 0 = v$, $v \cdot 1 = v$. A compiler applies them as rewrite rules alongside folding.

So with t1 = 3 * 2; t2 = x + 3; t3 = t1 + t1; t4 = x * 0; t5 = t1 - 2;, the constants are t1 = 6, t3 = 12, t4 = 0 (by the identity) and t5 = 4: four of five temporaries, while t2 depends on x. Yosys's opt_expr implements a set of such identities over its word-level cells, and also handles x bits, which may be chosen as either value to simplify further.

## Branches and sparse conditional propagation

Control flow limits plain propagation. If k = 9 + 3; and then if (k > 9) y = k * 3; else y = x + 1;, the phi for y at the join meets a constant (36) and an unknown, so plain propagation calls y unknown. But k folds to 12, so the condition is a constant true and the else arm can never run.

Sparse conditional constant propagation (SCCP), due to Wegman and Zadeck, tracks reachability and constants together. It marks only executable CFG edges, evaluates a branch condition to decide which successors become executable, and lets a phi meet only the values from executable predecessors. Here y = 36 and a later z = y + 1 folds to 37. The lattice has three levels per value (not yet known, a constant, not a constant), and the analysis runs to a fixed point exactly like other data-flow analyses.

## Going deeper

Wegman and Zadeck, "Constant Propagation with Conditional Branches" (TOPLAS 1991); the Yosys manual, opt_expr.

label: Common subexpression elimination
lesson:
# Common subexpression elimination

Common subexpression elimination (CSE) finds computations that produce a value already computed and reuses the earlier result. In software it saves instructions; in hardware it saves gates, because two identical cells with identical inputs can be merged into one. Value numbering is the standard way to find them, and Yosys's opt_merge and the structural hashing in AIG packages are the same idea on netlists.

## Local value numbering

Value numbering assigns a number to every distinct value. Inputs get fresh numbers. For each operation, form a key from its operator and its operands' value numbers, and look it up in a table. If the key is new, the result gets a fresh number and the key is recorded. If the key is present, the operation is redundant: the result is a copy of the earlier one and receives its number.

In t1 = b * c; t2 = c & t1; t3 = b - t2; t4 = t2 & b; t5 = b - t2;, the key for t5 (minus, number of b, number of t2) matches t3's, so t5 is replaced by a copy of t3: one redundant operation. Because a copy carries the original's value number, any later operation using t5 matches operations using t3, so savings cascade.

## Commutativity and canonical keys

a + b and b + a compute the same value, but their keys differ unless the compiler puts commutative operators into a canonical order, for example by sorting operand value numbers. With canonical keys, t7 = t1 & c matches an earlier t4 = c & t1. Subtraction is not commutative, so c - a and a - c keep different keys.

This is also where hardware compilers differ in strength. Structural hashing in an AIG canonicalizes the inputs of every AND node, so commuted duplicates merge automatically. Yosys's opt_merge compares cells by type, parameters and connected input signals, and handles commutative ports of cells such as add and and by normalizing their order. Deeper equivalences (a + b + c versus c + (a + b)) need algebraic rewriting or SAT-based sweeping, beyond what value numbering sees.

## Redefinition kills availability

Outside SSA, a variable can be reassigned, and then an expression that looks identical may not be. In t1 = a + b; a = t2; t3 = a + b;, the copy a = t2 gives a a new value number (that of t2), so t3's key differs from t1's and t3 is not redundant. Value numbering handles this automatically by updating the variable's number on every assignment; a text-matching approach would wrongly merge them.

In SSA this problem disappears, because a reassignment creates a new name, which is why compilers convert to SSA before CSE. In a netlist it never arises, since every net has one driver. The savings count is the number of operations whose result is replaced by a copy; in hardware each one is a cell removed, provided the merged cell's fan-out does not hurt timing, which is a trade-off a timing-driven flow may decide to reverse later by duplication.

## Going deeper

Cooper and Torczon, "Engineering a Compiler" (3rd ed.), chapter 8 (local value numbering); the Yosys manual, opt_merge.

label: Dead-code elimination
lesson:
# Dead-code elimination

Dead-code elimination (DCE) removes computations whose results cannot affect any output. In software that means instructions; in hardware it means cells, wires and registers left behind by constant folding, by unused outputs of IP blocks and by debug logic. Yosys runs it as opt_clean after almost every pass, and getting it right on cyclic hardware requires the mark-and-sweep form.

## Marking from the outputs

Mark-and-sweep DCE starts from what must be kept, the outputs (and any object marked keep), and walks backward through operands, marking each definition reached. Everything left unmarked is swept: it cannot influence an output on any path. With outputs depending on t6, which reads t4 and t5, which read t2 and t1, a temporary t3 that nothing marked reads is removed.

The walk is a graph search over use-def edges, linear in the size of the program. In a netlist the same search runs over nets and cells: start at the module's output ports and kept objects, and traverse from each cell's outputs back to its inputs. Unmarked cells and the wires that only they drive are deleted.

## Transitive dead code

Removing one dead statement can make others dead. If t3 = b & t1; and t4 = t2 + b; are both unused, removing them leaves t2 still used by t5, but in another program removing t4 might leave its operand t2 unused as well. A simple pass that deletes definitions with zero uses must therefore iterate until nothing changes; the marking approach gets the whole transitive set in one pass, because anything not reachable from an output is never marked.

This interacts with constant propagation. Folding a multiplexer select to a constant disconnects one input cone, which then becomes dead; folding a register to a constant disconnects its input logic. That is why synthesis scripts interleave opt_expr (folding) and opt_clean (sweeping) until a fixed point.

## Dead cycles in hardware

Hardware adds a case software DCE rarely meets: dead cycles. Two registers r1 <= r2 + a; and r2 <= r1 ^ b; that feed only each other each have a use, so a pass that removes only definitions with zero uses keeps both forever. Marking from the outputs never reaches them, so mark-and-sweep removes them correctly.

The opposite risk is removing logic that matters for reasons the IR does not show: a register observed only by a debug probe, a redundant flip-flop deliberately added for reliability, logic used by a formal property. Tools protect such objects with keep attributes or by treating properties and probes as outputs. A DCE implementation must define its roots precisely, because the roots, not the algorithm, decide what survives.

## Going deeper

Cooper and Torczon, "Engineering a Compiler", chapter 10; the Yosys manual, opt_clean.

label: Yosys RTLIL
lesson:
# Yosys RTLIL

RTLIL (RTL Intermediate Language) is the in-memory and textual IR of Yosys, the open-source synthesis framework. Every Yosys front end produces it, every pass transforms it and every back end writes from it, so it is the seam on which the whole tool is built. Understanding its objects is the prerequisite for reading Yosys logs, writing passes or plugging another front end into Yosys.

## Modules, wires, cells and connections

An RTLIL design is a set of modules. A module holds wires, cells, processes, memories and connections. A wire is just a named multi-bit signal with flags for being an input or output port; it stores nothing. A cell is an instance with a type, parameters and port connections: either an internal cell type, whose name begins with a dollar sign (such as the add, mux and dff cells), or a user module or black box.

Port connections use SigSpecs. A SigSpec is a concatenation of chunks, each a slice of a wire or a run of constant bits, so a cell input can connect to bits 7:4 of wire a followed by four constant zeros without any extra cells. Module-level connections join two SigSpecs directly, which is how plain assigns are represented.

## Coarse cells, fine cells and processes

Internal cells come in two grains. Coarse-grain cells are word-level operators parameterized by width and signedness, such as add with A_WIDTH, B_WIDTH, Y_WIDTH and A_SIGNED: one generic type covers every width, and passes read the parameters. Fine-grain cells are single-bit gates and flip-flops. Synthesis starts with coarse cells, then techmap lowers them to fine cells for ABC and technology mapping.

Two higher-level objects exist before lowering. Right after read_verilog, an always block is an RTLIL process: a decision tree of switch and case rules, plus sync rules for its clock edges. The proc passes later turn processes into multiplexer and flip-flop cells. Arrays become memory objects with read and write port cells, which the memory passes map to RAM resources or to flip-flops.

## Text format and attributes

write_rtlil prints a design in RTLIL text and read_rtlil reads it back exactly. This round trip is how pass development and debugging work: save the design before a suspicious pass, run the pass alone, diff the outputs. Regression tests for Yosys passes are often written as small RTLIL or Verilog inputs plus expected results.

Every object carries attributes. The src attribute records the source file and line, and it travels with cells through passes so that reports point back at RTL. The keep attribute tells cleanup passes not to remove an object even if nothing reads it; keep_hierarchy tells flatten to leave a module's boundary. Because RTLIL is the stable shared IR, a plug-in pass written against it works for designs from Verilog, from VHDL through GHDL or from SystemVerilog through slang or Surelog front ends.

## Going deeper

Wolf, the Yosys manual, chapters on RTLIL and internal cell types; the Yosys source, kernel/rtlil.h.

label: The Yosys proc passes
lesson:
# The Yosys proc passes

The proc passes are where Yosys turns procedural HDL code into a netlist. Every always block arrives as an RTLIL process, and proc converts its decision tree into multiplexers and its clock and reset structure into flip-flops and latches. Latch inference, reset recognition and the shape of the initial netlist are all decided here, which makes proc the first place to look when synthesis output surprises you.

## From processes to cells

A process holds a decision tree, built from the if and case statements, and sync rules that say when assignments take effect (on a clock edge, or always for combinational code). proc lowers it to cells: each signal's final value through the decision tree becomes a tree of multiplexer cells, and each sync rule on an edge becomes a flip-flop whose D input is that multiplexer tree. An always @(posedge clk) process therefore becomes a dff cell fed by muxes.

Running proc early matters, because the optimization passes (opt_expr, opt_merge, opt_clean) work on cells and nets, and a process is still procedural. Every standard synthesis script runs proc right after reading and checking the hierarchy.

## The sub-passes

proc is a sequence of smaller passes. proc_clean and proc_rmdead remove empty parts of processes and decision-tree branches that can never be taken. proc_init turns initial values into init attributes on wires, which FPGA flows honor. proc_arst looks for an asynchronous reset: a top-level if on a signal that also appears as an edge in the sensitivity list, and rewrites it so that a flip-flop with asynchronous reset can be built. proc_mux converts the decision trees into multiplexer cells. proc_dlatch creates latches for signals a combinational process does not assign on every path. proc_dff creates flip-flops for the edge-triggered sync rules.

Each step has a narrow job, and the order matters: reset detection must happen before the flip-flops are built, and latch creation needs the multiplexer structure to know which paths leave a signal unassigned.

## Reading what proc produced

A latch cell in the log after proc means some output of a block meant to be combinational is not assigned on every path; proc_dlatch only creates one when a value must hold. A missing reset pin on a flip-flop that should have one usually means proc_arst did not recognize an unusual reset coding style, so the reset ended up in the data path.

Blocking assignments to temporaries are tracked through the decision tree, so later reads use the newly assigned value, much like SSA renaming; the temporary becomes plain logic unless it is read before it is written, in which case it is a flip-flop. The multiplexer trees proc builds are a direct translation and often redundant, with branches assigning the same value or controlled by constants, so the opt passes that follow (opt_muxtree, opt_expr, opt_clean) usually shrink them a lot.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual, the proc command and its sub-passes; Wolf, "Yosys Open SYnthesis Suite" documentation, chapter on the synthesis flow.

label: Yosys opt passes and flatten
lesson:
# Yosys opt passes and flatten

Yosys's opt command is a fixed-point loop of netlist optimizations that implement, on RTLIL cells, the classical compiler optimizations: constant folding, common subexpression elimination and dead-code elimination, plus hardware-specific passes for multiplexer trees and flip-flops. Flatten decides how far those optimizations can reach. Knowing which pass does what lets you read a synthesis log and design a flow.

## Folding, merging and cleaning

Three passes map directly onto compiler optimizations. opt_expr performs constant folding and simple algebraic rewrites: a cell with constant inputs is evaluated, and patterns such as AND with 0 or a multiplexer with equal inputs are simplified. opt_merge is common subexpression elimination on the netlist: cells with the same type, the same parameters and the same input signals compute the same value, so one is kept and drives both sets of loads. opt_clean is dead-code elimination: it removes cells and wires that drive nothing used, keeping ports and objects with the keep attribute.

Each pass exposes work for the others. Folding can make two cells identical, merging can leave a cell without loads, and cleaning can simplify fan-in so that more folding applies. The opt command therefore repeats its sub-passes until none of them changes the design.

## Multiplexers and flip-flops

Hardware adds passes with no direct software analogue. opt_muxtree removes multiplexer inputs that can never be selected: in a tree of multiplexers sharing a select signal, an inner multiplexer on the same select along one branch has an unreachable input. opt_reduce simplifies reduce and multiplexer cells, for example removing duplicate inputs of a wide OR.

opt_dff works on flip-flops. A flip-flop whose D input is a constant equal to its reset or initial value can only ever hold that value, so it becomes a constant. A feedback multiplexer in front of a flip-flop, D = en ? x : Q, is folded into a flip-flop with an enable, and synchronous reset logic is folded into a flip-flop with a synchronous reset, matching cells that libraries and FPGAs provide directly.

## Flattening and pass ordering

Optimization stops at module boundaries: a constant tied to a submodule's input cannot propagate inside while the boundary exists. flatten inlines submodules into their parents so that constants and duplicates become visible across former boundaries; modules marked keep_hierarchy, and black boxes, stay as instances. After flattening, two copies of one submodule tied to different constants are optimized differently, which is exactly the divergence that uniquification would otherwise have to handle.

Script order matters. A typical flow reads the design, checks the hierarchy, runs proc, optionally flattens, runs opt, extracts FSMs and memories, runs opt again, lowers with techmap, runs opt once more and hands the result to ABC. Running opt only once, before techmap, would leave the constant and duplicate gates that techmap creates when it expands word-level cells.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual, the opt, opt_expr, opt_merge, opt_clean, opt_muxtree, opt_dff and flatten commands, and the synth command's script.

lesson:
# Open-source HDL front ends

Open-source EDA has several HDL front ends, each with a different scope: event-driven simulators, compiled simulators, VHDL tools, full SystemVerilog compilers and shared elaborated databases. A tool designer must know which front end to build on, what each gets right and how they connect, because a flow's language coverage is only as good as the front end it uses.

## The main tools and their roles

Icarus Verilog compiles Verilog with iverilog into an intermediate form, vvp code, that the vvp runtime simulates event by event with four-state values; it is close to the standard's scheduling model. Verilator translates Verilog and SystemVerilog into a C++ (or SystemC) model that is compiled with a testbench into a fast, statically scheduled, two-state simulator; it is also a widely used linter. GHDL analyzes, compiles and simulates VHDL with several code-generation back ends, and offers synthesis through a Yosys plug-in.

slang is a C++ library and compiler front end for SystemVerilog that aims at complete parsing, type checking and elaboration, with precise diagnostics; other tools use it as their front end. Surelog parses and elaborates SystemVerilog and writes the result as UHDM. Yosys has its own read_verilog, which covers Verilog-2005 and part of SystemVerilog.

## Front-end architecture and shared models

Every Verilog front end runs the same phases: preprocessing (macros, includes and ifdef), lexing and parsing, then elaboration (hierarchy, parameters and generate), then type checking and lowering into the tool's IR. Elaboration is where SystemVerilog is hardest and where tools diverge most.

UHDM (Universal Hardware Data Model) attacks that duplication. It is a serialized object model of a fully elaborated SystemVerilog design, based on the standard's VPI object model. Surelog produces it, and consumers such as a Yosys plug-in read it, so each consumer gets one shared elaborated design instead of parsing SystemVerilog itself. A Yosys plug-in built on slang does the same job by another route, translating slang's elaborated model into RTLIL; CIRCT's SystemVerilog import also builds on slang.

## Choosing and cross-checking front ends

Front ends differ widely in language coverage, and a shared conformance suite, sv-tests, makes the gaps visible by running thousands of small SystemVerilog examples through each tool and recording which parse, elaborate or simulate correctly. Verible is a separate family of parser-based tools for lint, formatting and indexing, which work on the syntax tree without full elaboration.

Running RTL through two independent front ends is cheap insurance. When Icarus and Verilator disagree, or a lint warning about width appears in one tool only, the cause is usually real: a truncated expression, a race or behavior that depends on x. Differential testing across independent implementations is the same idea as differential testing of an engine change, applied to the language itself.

## Going deeper

The documentation of Icarus Verilog, Verilator, GHDL, slang, Surelog and UHDM; the CHIPS Alliance sv-tests dashboard.

label: Verilator's compiled cycle model
lesson:
# Verilator's compiled cycle model

Verilator is the fastest open-source Verilog simulator because it is a compiler: it turns RTL into C++ that evaluates the design in a statically chosen order with two-state values. That design choice explains both its speed and its differences from event-driven simulators, and it makes Verilator a natural engine for automated compile-and-simulate loops.

## A compiled, two-state model

An event-driven simulator such as Icarus keeps an event queue and evaluates processes as their inputs change. Verilator instead analyzes the whole design, orders its logic statically and emits C++ classes whose eval function computes the next state of the design in that fixed order. There is no event-queue overhead, and the generated code is compiled with full optimization.

Values are two-state by default: each bit is 0 or 1, mapping directly onto machine integers, and x and z are resolved to concrete values. In the classic flow the user writes a C++ (or SystemC) main loop that sets inputs, toggles the clock and calls eval; newer releases can also build a standalone binary from a Verilog testbench. With --lint-only, Verilator runs its front end and checks without building a model, which makes it a popular linter.

## Scheduling, warnings and threads

Static ordering must still respect the language. Verilator orders the computation so that all clocked blocks read pre-edge values before any register is updated, reproducing nonblocking semantics with ordering and shadow variables. Combinational logic is sorted by dependency. When the dependency graph appears cyclic, often because different bits of one vector feed each other, Verilator warns UNOPTFLAT and must iterate that part of the logic until it converges, which slows the model.

For speed on large designs, Verilator partitions the logic into tasks with dependencies and schedules them across threads. With its timing option, it supports delays and event controls by compiling processes into C++ coroutines, so ordinary Verilog testbenches with delays can run; without it, such constructs are not modeled.

## Where Verilator differs from four-state simulators

Two-state modeling can hide bugs. A register with no reset that reaches an output shows x in a four-state simulator but a concrete value in Verilator, so a design can pass in Verilator and fail elsewhere. Teams randomize initial values across regression runs (with the x-initial and x-assign options) so that logic silently depending on power-up zeros is caught.

Racy code is the other source of differences. The standard leaves the order of same-time processes open, so Verilator's static order and an event-driven simulator's order can both be legal and still disagree; the fix belongs in the code. For automated RTL loops Verilator is attractive: strict diagnostics and very fast runs, with the C++ compile step as the main latency to manage, for example with a compiler cache and incremental builds.

## Going deeper

Snyder, the Verilator manual; the Verilator documentation on scheduling and the timing option.

lesson:
# MLIR and CIRCT

MLIR is a compiler infrastructure for building IRs at many abstraction levels in one framework; CIRCT (Circuit IR Compilers and Tools) applies it to hardware. Together they turn the classical ideas of this domain, SSA, dominance and passes, into reusable infrastructure for hardware compilers, and they are the main candidate substrate for compilers that agents can extend safely.

## Operations, regions and block arguments

In MLIR everything is an operation: an addition, a function and a whole module are all operations, with operands, results, attributes (compile-time constants such as widths or names) and optionally regions. A region is a list of blocks nested inside an operation, such as the body of a function, and each block is a list of operations ending in a terminator. Operations are grouped into dialects, namespaces of operations, types and attributes for one abstraction level or domain, such as arith, scf, llvm, or CIRCT's hw and comb.

MLIR is SSA, but it has no phi operation. Instead, blocks take arguments, and each branch passes values to its successor's arguments. A block argument is exactly a phi, placed by the same dominance-frontier reasoning, with the edge-to-value pairing written at each branch rather than collected at the join.

## Passes, patterns and progressive lowering

MLIR compilers are pipelines of passes. Many passes are built from rewrite patterns: local rules that match an operation and replace it. Canonicalization collects each operation's folders and simplification patterns into one cleanup pass applied to a fixed point. The dialect conversion framework lowers between dialects: the author supplies patterns plus a conversion target that declares which operations are legal afterwards, and the framework applies patterns until every illegal operation is gone or reports what could not be converted.

Progressive lowering is the resulting style: a program moves step by step through dialects of decreasing abstraction, each step small and testable. After every pass a verifier checks structural rules, such as operand types and dominance. Verification catches malformed IR; it does not prove that a pass preserved meaning, which needs tests or formal equivalence.

## CIRCT for hardware

CIRCT builds hardware compilers on this infrastructure. Its core dialects describe structure, combinational logic and state; other dialects cover FIRRTL, SystemVerilog emission, dataflow and high-level synthesis. Hardware module bodies are graph regions, where the dominance requirement of ordinary SSA regions is dropped, so an operation may use a value defined later in the block: feedback through registers is written directly.

Several tools ship with CIRCT. firtool compiles FIRRTL, as emitted by Chisel, into SystemVerilog. A SystemVerilog import built on slang brings Verilog into CIRCT dialects. arcilator compiles designs through the Arc dialect into fast native simulation code, and equivalence and bounded model checking tools work on the same IR. The shared infrastructure means a pass written once, with its tests, serves all of these flows.

## Going deeper

Lattner et al., "MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure for Domain Specific Computation" (CGO 2021); the CIRCT documentation and rationale documents.

lesson:
# CIRCT dialects: HW, Comb, Seq and lowering

CIRCT represents hardware with a family of MLIR dialects, each capturing one concern: structure, combinational logic, state, SystemVerilog emission and several higher-level models. A hardware compiler built on CIRCT is a sequence of lowerings between them. Knowing what each dialect holds is what lets you read CIRCT IR, choose where a transformation belongs and follow a design from Chisel or SystemVerilog to emitted Verilog.

## HW, Comb and Seq

Three core dialects describe a synchronous circuit. hw holds structure: hw.module with ports, hw.instance, hw.output and hw.constant, plus aggregate types such as arrays and structs. comb holds side-effect-free combinational operations on integer types: add, mul, mux, icmp, concat, extract and the bitwise operators. seq holds state: register operations such as seq.compreg and seq.firreg, and the clock type.

Comb integers are signless, following MLIR's convention: an i8 is just 8 bits. Signedness lives in the operations that care about it, such as the predicate of icmp (slt versus ult) or the choice between signed and unsigned division. This removes a whole class of Verilog sizing and signedness ambiguities from the IR.

## SV, ExportVerilog and the lowering path

The sv dialect sits just above Verilog text. It has operations for SystemVerilog-specific constructs, such as always blocks, regs, wires, assigns and ifdef, used to control what the emitted code looks like. ExportVerilog prints hw, comb, seq and sv operations as SystemVerilog, choosing names and expression layout so that downstream simulators, linters and synthesis tools accept it.

A Chisel design flows firrtl, then hw with comb and seq, then sv, then Verilog text. Registers stay as seq operations rather than being lowered early to always blocks, because analyses and optimizations can reason about a register operation directly without recognizing a procedural idiom; only near the end do they become sv constructs for printing.

## Higher-level and simulation dialects

Other dialects capture other models of hardware. handshake describes latency-insensitive dataflow with ready-valid channels, used by flows that compile software-like programs into circuits. calyx is the IR of the Calyx compiler for accelerators: components with structural groups and an explicit control schedule. llhd (low-level hardware description) has signals, processes and time, matching event-driven HDL simulation semantics. moore captures SystemVerilog semantics coming out of the slang-based importer before they are lowered to the core dialects. arc models state transfers for the arcilator simulator.

Each sits at a different point between source semantics and netlist, and progressive lowering connects them. Choosing the dialect at which to implement a transformation is the main architectural decision when extending CIRCT: as high as the information it needs, as low as the simplicity it wants.

## Going deeper

The CIRCT documentation for the HW, Comb, Seq, SV, Handshake, Calyx, LLHD, Moore and Arc dialects; Nigam et al., "A Compiler Infrastructure for Accelerator Generators" (ASPLOS 2021).

lesson:
# FIRRTL and its lowering

FIRRTL (Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL) is the IR between Chisel and Verilog. Chisel elaborates a circuit and emits FIRRTL; a FIRRTL compiler infers widths and resets, resolves conditional connections, flattens aggregate types and emits Verilog. Its passes are a compact case study in hardware-compiler lowering, now implemented in CIRCT's firtool.

## Circuits, connections and widths

A FIRRTL circuit contains modules with ports, wires, registers, nodes and memories, and statements that connect them. Conditional connections appear in when blocks; after lowering, each becomes a multiplexer selecting between the connections made inside and outside the block. Aggregate types (bundles and vectors) describe structured ports, and a flipped field in a bundle flows in the opposite direction to the rest, as ready does in a valid-ready interface.

Widths may be left unspecified. Width inference computes the minimal widths that satisfy every expression and connection, using the primitive operations' width rules: add is lossless, so adding an 8-bit and a 5-bit UInt gives $\max(8, 5) + 1 = 9$ bits, and multiplication gives the sum of the widths.

## The lowering passes

A handful of passes take FIRRTL from Chisel's output to netlist form. InferWidths fixes every unspecified width. InferResets resolves abstract reset types to synchronous or asynchronous resets from how they are driven. ExpandWhens implements last-connect semantics: it turns nested conditional connections into one multiplexer expression per signal, so that afterwards every sink has a single driving expression. LowerTypes splits bundles and vectors into individual ground-type signals with derived names, because Verilog ports and wires are ground types.

After these passes the circuit is essentially a netlist of primitive operations, registers and memories, which maps directly onto CIRCT's hw, comb and seq dialects for optimization and Verilog export.

## Initialization, invalidation and annotations

FIRRTL enforces that every sink is driven on every path. A wire that is never connected, or connected only under some conditions, is reported as not fully initialized, which turns a forgotten connection into a compile error rather than a silent x in simulation. Marking a signal invalid (DontCare in Chisel) is an explicit don't-care: the compiler may choose any value, which can simplify logic, much like assigning x in Verilog for synthesis.

Annotations carry metadata alongside the circuit, targeting specific components: don't-touch markers that protect signals from optimization, memory configuration, or hooks for verification and test. Current Chisel uses the CIRCT-based firtool, the MLIR FIRRTL compiler, which replaced the original Scala FIRRTL compiler; the passes above now live in CIRCT's FIRRTL dialect.

## Going deeper

Izraelevitz et al., "Reusability is FIRRTL Ground: Hardware Construction Languages, Compiler Frameworks, and Transformations" (ICCAD 2017); the FIRRTL specification; the CIRCT FIRRTL dialect documentation.

# Compile-and-simulate loops for agent-written RTL

Agents that write and refactor RTL work inside a harness: a loop that compiles, lints, simulates and synthesizes each candidate and feeds the results back. The harness, not the model, decides what counts as success, so its design determines whether an agent produces working hardware or code that merely passes the checks it was shown. This concept applies the edit-build-test loop to HDL engines concretely.

## The loop and its order of checks

A request arrives, the model proposes an RTL edit, and the harness writes it and runs checks in increasing order of cost: lint and compile first (seconds), then unit simulation tests, then synthesis checks and equivalence or formal checks. A failure at any stage goes back to the model and the loop repeats; when everything passes, the diff and the evidence go to a human reviewer.

Cheap failures first is the rule, because a width or syntax error found in seconds makes a ten-minute regression pointless. Iteration speed bounds how many attempts an agent gets, so the build step deserves engineering: if 3.5 of every 4 minutes are spent recompiling a Verilator model, a compiler cache, incremental builds of changed modules or an interpreted simulator for the inner loop pay off more than anything else. A fast strict engine (Verilator) in the inner loop and an accurate four-state simulator as a later gate is the fast-versus-accurate pattern applied to simulation.

## What feedback to return

The model can only fix what the feedback describes. For a compile failure, return the diagnostic verbatim: file, line, construct and error class. For a simulation failure, return the failing test, the first mismatching cycle, the expected and actual values and the signals involved, not the whole waveform database. A minimal counterexample is what a human would debug from, and it fits in a context window.

The harness also decides which diagnostics block acceptance. Synthesis findings matter even when simulation passes: an inferred latch means some path leaves an output unassigned, which the tests did not cover, so the harness should fail the candidate and return the latch report. Width-truncation lint is worth gating for the same reason. Hidden or held-out tests, and equivalence against a reference, catch an agent that special-cases the visible tests' inputs.

## Failure modes and acceptance

Generated RTL and testbenches can hang, through a combinational loop or a missing finish, or exhaust memory, so simulations run in a sandbox with time and memory limits that turn a hang into a reportable failure. An agent that oscillates between two edits, each fixing one test and breaking another, needs the loop to detect the cycle, stop and present both failures together.

Acceptance stays with a human, who reviews the diff with its evidence: tests passed, lint clean, synthesis report, equivalence result. Measuring the agent is part of the design too: the fraction of tasks whose final RTL compiles, passes hidden tests and is free of blocking lint and synthesis issues says far more than compile-pass rate or lines generated.

## Going deeper

The Verilator manual on lint and build options; the agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum on the harness loop and change tiers.

lesson:
# Proving an agent's RTL refactor

When an agent refactors RTL, passing the existing tests is not proof that behavior is unchanged. What must be proven depends on the kind of change: renaming needs only combinational equivalence, re-encoding needs sequential equivalence, pipelining needs equivalence up to latency, and an intended bug fix needs proof that behavior moved only where intended. This concept turns golden and differential testing into concrete RTL obligations.

## Golden and differential tests

A golden test is a fixed stimulus with recorded known-good outputs, compared after every change: any behavioral change, intended or not, becomes visible. A differential simulation drives the old and new versions with the same stimulus and compares outputs cycle by cycle; it needs no expected values, because the old design is the reference.

Both only cover the stimulus applied. A difference on an input sequence never simulated survives. That is why the reference must be the last approved version, not the agent's previous attempt, so errors cannot accumulate across iterations, and why simulation is paired with formal methods where the change allows it. For a pure rename or reformat, where registers correspond one to one, a combinational equivalence check with registers matched by name or position is cheap and complete.

## Choosing the equivalence method

The method follows from what the refactor did to state. If registers still correspond, compare the combinational logic between them; open-source flows do this with Yosys, reading both designs and proving equivalence with equiv_make, equiv_simple and equiv_induct, or with a SAT-based miter. If the agent re-encoded a state machine from binary to one-hot, the registers no longer correspond, and only sequential equivalence, which reasons over input sequences from reset, applies.

If the agent pipelined a combinational multiplier into two stages, outputs now appear one cycle later, so equivalence holds only against the original delayed by one cycle, and the check must say so. Counterexamples that appear only when an input is x usually mean the two versions treat don't-cares differently; constraints on the inputs decide whether that matters.

## Intended changes and quality

Not every change should preserve behavior. For an intended fix, such as an off-by-one in a counter's wrap value, the differential proof must show that outputs differ only in the cycles where the counter wraps and match everywhere else: the analogue of a differential timing report showing that only the intended paths moved. A refactor of a module instantiated in 40 places with different parameters must be checked for each distinct parameterization actually used, since each is separate hardware.

Correct is not the same as acceptable. A refactor that passes equivalence but grows synthesized area by 12 percent is a quality regression, and the harness should report it beside the equivalence pass. Every engine change in an agent-first flow ships with both kinds of check: function against a reference and quality against a baseline.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual, equiv_make, equiv_simple, equiv_induct and miter; Kuehlmann and van Eijk, "Combinational and Sequential Equivalence Checking" in "Logic Synthesis and Verification" (2002).

label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL generation
lesson:
# Tool-grounded rewards for RTL generation

Training models to write RTL with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the most reliable rewards come from tools: compilers, simulators, equivalence checkers and synthesis. A tool-grounded reward is deterministic and checkable, but every tool has blind spots, and a model optimized hard against them will find them. Designing the reward is therefore an exercise in knowing exactly what each tool does and does not check.

## Components of a grounded reward

A tool-grounded reward scores generated RTL with deterministic tools against a ground truth: does it compile, does it pass a held-out testbench or prove equivalent to a reference, does it synthesize without latches or errors, and what area and timing does synthesis report. Each component measures something different. Compile success is necessary but nearly worthless alone, because a module that outputs zero compiles, and a model rewarded only for compiling learns to emit safe, useless code.

Correctness needs a reference behavior, from tests or from equivalence checking, and quality terms must be gated on correctness. If smaller area scores higher regardless, the model learns to delete functionality the tests do not exercise.

## Reward hacking

A model maximizes what the reward measures, not what was meant. If the testbench is visible during generation, the model can special-case the stimulus. If it learns that adding a full_case pragma reduces area while the simulation tests still pass, it exploits a gap between the synthesis assumption and the simulation check. If simulation is two-state, a register with no reset reaching an output never shows as x, so the missing reset goes unpunished.

Each hack points at a defense. Regenerate constrained random stimulus for every evaluation so that memorizing it does not help; add formal checks where a reference exists; check four-state behavior or randomize initial values; lint for pragmas and other constructs that change synthesis semantics without being checked. The reward is only as honest as its least careful checker.

## Fast proxies and signoff

Accurate evaluation is expensive. Full place-and-route and signoff timing for every sample would make training unaffordable, so rewards use fast proxies, such as Yosys area estimates or a quick timing estimate. The gap between proxy and signoff quality is where optimization drifts: a model can learn structures that score well on the proxy and poorly after routing.

Two practices contain the drift. Periodically evaluate a sample of outputs with the accurate flow and check that proxy improvements still track real ones, the same fast-versus-accurate pattern used in design loops. Version and pin every tool in the reward, because a tool update that changes results for identical outputs corrupts the learning signal. For benchmarks, tasks drawn from real modules with hidden tests and synthesis checks separate useful models far better than short textbook exercises or prompts that include their own tests.

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum on tool-grounded reinforcement learning; published RTL-generation benchmarks with hidden testbenches.
